title: Temperature dependence and coupling of dissolved oxygen and pH in coastal habitats
content:
by Alexandra Steckbauer, Iris E. Hendriks, Raquel Vaquer-Sunyer, Vincent Saderne, Andrea Anton, Dorte Krause-Jensen, Susana Agusti, Carlos M. Duarte

Coastal waters experience daily fluctuations in oxygen (O2), carbon dioxide (CO2), and pH driven by respiration and photosynthesis, processes that are highly sensitive to temperature variations. As global temperatures continue to rise, both photosynthetic and respiratory rates are increasing, with respiration accelerating more rapidly. The resulting decline in photosynthetic oxygen production and CO2 uptake relative to respiratory oxygen demand and CO2 release is leading to widespread declines in oxygen availability and heightened acidification of coastal ecosystems, particularly in warmer regions. Here, we investigate the variability and co-variance of O2 and pH in diverse coastal habitats and their temperature dependence, utilizing a comprehensive dataset of 516,705 data points spanning a temperature gradient of 1–39°C. Our in situ data capture a wide range of ecosystems, including seagrass meadows, micro-, macro-, and filamentous algae, mangrove forests, kelp forests, coral reefs, and bare sediments, from polar to tropical regions across both hemispheres. We show that rising temperatures are associated with decreases in O2 and pH, alongside amplified diel fluctuations in these parameters, increasing the prevalence of daytime hypoxia and hyperoxia. Furthermore, our data reveal a strong correlation between O2 and pH, driven by photosynthetic and respiratory activity, with temperature and across diverse ecosystems and geographic regions. These findings are also relevant for the design of laboratory experiments focused on temperature stressors or simulations of marine heatwaves and emphasize the need for establishing localized baseline data on environmental conditions and water chemistry. The temperature-dependent relationship and co-variation between dissolved oxygen (DO) and pH in metabolic hotspots, such as coastal vegetated ecosystems, underscore the importance of diurnal variability in shaping DO and pH thresholds critical for supporting biodiversity.
author: Alexandra Steckbauer
